title: DOES THE BIBLE TEACH SEXUAL ENTITLEMENT IN MARRIAGE—or Mutuality?
paragraphs: DOES THE BIBLE TEACH SEXUAL ENTITLEMENT IN MARRIAGE—or Mutuality?
What if the verse someone used to demand your body was actually written to destroy selfishness—not defend it?
There are Bible verses that have comforted wounded people.
There are Bible verses that have brought marriages back from the edge.

And then there are Bible verses that wounded people have heard while sitting in silence, wondering whether God Himself expected them to surrender their dignity just to prove they were a “good spouse.”
One of those passages is 1 Corinthians 7.
Maybe you have heard it quoted like this:
“Your body doesn’t belong to you anymore.”
Perhaps those words were spoken gently in a sermon about marital intimacy.
Perhaps they were spoken during an argument.
Perhaps they were used as leverage.
Perhaps you were made to feel guilty because you were exhausted, grieving, sick, frightened, emotionally disconnected, recovering from childbirth, carrying trauma, or simply struggling.
Or perhaps you were the spouse doing the demanding.
You never thought of yourself as cruel.
You simply believed marriage meant your husband or wife owed you sexual access.
After all...
doesn’t the Bible say so?
This is where we need enough courage to stop repeating fragments of Scripture and actually listen to Paul.
Because something extraordinary happens when 1 Corinthians 7:3–5 is allowed to speak in its own context.
Paul does talk about marital obligation.
Paul does talk about the body.
Paul does tell married believers not to deprive one another carelessly.
We should not erase those truths simply because modern ears find them uncomfortable.
But Paul does something that would have been remarkably striking in the ancient world.
He turns the entire argument in both directions.
Not once.
Repeatedly.
Listen to the rhythm.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 7:3 begins:
“τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ ἀνδρί.”
Transliterated:
Tē gynaiki ho anēr tēn opheilēn apodidotō, homoiōs de kai hē gynē tō andri.
In straightforward English:
Let the husband give to his wife what is due to her, and likewise the wife to her husband.
Notice where Paul begins.
Not:
“Husbands, collect what your wives owe you.”
Not:
“Wives, your husband purchased permanent access to your body when you married him.”
Not even:
“One spouse has needs; the other exists to satisfy them.”
Paul begins with giving.
Then comes the statement people often remember:
“ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ...”
The wife does not exercise authority over her own body, but her husband does.
Someone could stop there.
And tragically, some do.
But Paul does not stop there.
The sentence continues with a devastating symmetry:
“ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.”
“Likewise,” Paul says, the husband does not exercise authority over his own body, but his wife does.
The key verb is related to ἐξουσιάζω — exousiazō, meaning to exercise authority or have authority over something.
And Paul deliberately applies the principle both ways.
Wife toward husband.
Husband toward wife.
Her body is not a commodity he owns.
His body is not a commodity she owns.
Instead, Christian marriage creates an astonishing relationship of reciprocal belonging.
That distinction changes everything.
Because if you read only half the verse, you can turn marriage into entitlement.
Read the whole passage, and entitlement begins collapsing under the weight of mutuality.
The person demanding, “Your body belongs to me,” must confront the other half of Paul's argument:
Then yours belongs in service to your spouse too.
Your comfort.
Your patience.
Your gentleness.
Your restraint.
Your sacrifice.
Your concern for their wellbeing.
Your body cannot become the instrument through which you selfishly dominate the person to whom you have supposedly given yourself.
That is precisely why this passage cannot honestly be reduced to, “My spouse owes me sex whenever I want it.”
Paul's language is reciprocal.
His concern is reciprocal.
Even the temporary abstinence he discusses in 1 Corinthians 7:5 is described in terms of agreement—“by mutual consent” for a time, followed by reunion.
Marriage does not turn selfishness holy merely because selfishness is wearing a wedding ring.
And maybe somebody needed to hear that sentence tonight.
Because somewhere there is a wife wondering whether saying, “I'm hurting,” makes her rebellious.
Somewhere there is a husband carrying rejection so deeply that resentment has begun eating him alive.
Somewhere two Christians sleep inches apart while emotionally living miles away.
Somewhere someone has been weaponizing Scripture.
Somewhere someone else has been withholding affection as punishment.
Both need Jesus.
Because biblical mutuality does not mean sexual intimacy becomes irrelevant.
It means intimacy is rescued from selfishness.
Paul does not teach spouses to weaponize withholding against each other. His language in 1 Corinthians 7 takes marital sexual responsibility seriously.
But taking marital intimacy seriously is not the same thing as granting one spouse permission to disregard the humanity of the other.
There is a world of difference between:
“I give myself to you because I love you”
and
“You must give yourself to me because I own you.”
One sounds like covenant.
The other sounds like possession.
And Christian marriage was never designed to be possession.
It was designed to become a living picture of covenant love.
That is why another famous marriage passage begins its household instructions with:
“Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.”
Then Paul tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her. He later tells husbands to love their wives as their own bodies.
Think about the standard.
Christ.
Not lust.
Christ.
Not domination.
Christ.
Not manipulation.
Christ.
And what did Christ do?
He gave Himself.
The cross is not the picture of Jesus screaming, “Give Me what I deserve!”
The cross shows the Son of God laying Himself down in sacrificial love to redeem His people.
So when a Christian husband invokes “biblical authority” while ignoring Christlike sacrifice, he has separated authority from the very Gospel that defines Christian leadership.

And when either spouse treats intimacy as a bargaining chip—rewarding obedience, punishing disagreement, manipulating affection, deliberately humiliating the other—the marriage is drifting away from the self-giving love Scripture calls believers toward.
Sexual intimacy within Christian marriage was never meant to become a courtroom where husband and wife argue about who owes whom.
It belongs in a covenant where two people increasingly learn to say:
How can I love you?
How can I understand you?
What are you carrying that I have not noticed?
Where have I become selfish?
Where have I made you feel unwanted?
Where have I made you feel used?

Where have resentment, pornography, infidelity, exhaustion, childbirth, illness, trauma, shame, insecurity, unresolved conflict, or years of emotional neglect entered our bedroom before either of us did?
Those questions are harder than quoting a verse.
Because verses can be used as shields.
Questions require us to become vulnerable.
Maybe the deepest problem in your marriage isn't frequency.
Maybe it is safety.
Maybe it isn't desire.
Maybe it is resentment.
Maybe your spouse does not primarily need another argument about sex.
Maybe they need an apology.
Maybe you do.
Maybe you need counseling.
Maybe you need repentance.
Maybe you need to confess the pornography you keep hiding.
Maybe you need to admit that rejection has made you bitter.
Maybe you need to stop treating your spouse like a machine that exists to regulate your emotions.
Maybe you need to stop using withdrawal to punish someone you promised to love.
Maybe you both need to kneel beside the same bed where so much tension has lived and finally say:
“Jesus, we cannot heal this without You.”
Because this conversation is ultimately bigger than sex.
It is about what sin does to love.
Sin takes gifts and turns them into demands.
Sin takes desire and turns it into entitlement.
Sin takes leadership and turns it into domination.
Sin takes vulnerability and turns it into leverage.
Sin takes hurt and turns it into revenge.
Sin whispers:
“What can I get?”
Jesus teaches another way:
“How can I love?”
And that is where the scandal of grace enters the bedroom.
Not as permission to ignore wounds.
Not as religious language pasted over abuse.
Not as a command to pretend everything is fine.
Grace tells the truth.
Grace exposes selfishness.
Grace confronts sin.
Grace protects what is precious.
Grace forgives the repentant.
Grace teaches sinners how to love again.
And sometimes grace begins with the most difficult sentence a married person can say:
“I was wrong.”
Maybe you demanded when you should have listened.
“I was wrong.”
Maybe you withheld affection to punish.
“I was wrong.”
Maybe pornography trained your imagination to consume bodies instead of cherish a person.
“I was wrong.”
Maybe you quoted Scripture to win arguments instead of submitting yourself to Scripture so Christ could change you.
“I was wrong.”
Those words can feel humiliating.
But confession is not the funeral of a Christian marriage.
Sometimes it is where resurrection begins.
Jesus specializes in meeting sinners precisely where the truth finally breaks through the pretending.
Peter failed.
David fell catastrophically.
The Corinthian church itself was filled with sexual confusion and moral disorder.
Yet the Gospel kept calling sinners out of darkness.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because the blood of Christ mattered more.
Paul tells the Corinthians that believers were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending you were never stained.
Being washed.
Not pretending you never failed.
Being forgiven.
Not defending selfishness.
Repenting of it.
And repentance means more than crying because consequences hurt.
Repentance turns around.
The husband who has treated intimacy as entitlement learns tenderness.
The wife who has deliberately weaponized rejection learns honesty and mercy.
The spouse trapped in pornography brings darkness into the light and seeks serious accountability.
The couple buried under years of resentment stops pretending Sunday smiles can substitute for healing.

And where coercion, threats, violence, sexual assault, or abuse are present, “submit more” is not a responsible substitute for safety, truth, pastoral wisdom, professional help, and, when appropriate, civil authorities.
Marriage is not permission to sin against another human being.
A wedding covenant does not make cruelty righteous.
Jesus never needs evil in order to defend marriage.
He calls evil into the light.
So does the Bible teach sexual entitlement in marriage?

If by “entitlement” we mean that one spouse may selfishly demand sexual access while disregarding the other spouse's wellbeing, dignity, suffering, or humanity, 1 Corinthians 7 cannot honestly bear that weight.
What it gives us instead is something more demanding.
Mutual responsibility.
Mutual belonging.
Mutual consideration.
Mutual generosity.
Mutual vulnerability.
A husband who belongs to his wife.
A wife who belongs to her husband.
Two bodies.
Two sinners.
One covenant.
Both standing beneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That is harder than entitlement.
Entitlement asks only what the other person owes me.
Covenant asks what love requires of me.
And perhaps that is why this teaching cuts so deeply.
Because somewhere between the wedding photographs and the unpaid bills...
between babies and sleepless nights...
between careers and disappointments...
between arguments nobody remembers starting and wounds nobody knows how to finish...
we can forget that the person beside us is not an object.
That is somebody Christ calls you to love.
A soul.
A person bearing God's image.
Someone with fears you may not understand.
Someone with wounds they may struggle to explain.
Someone who may desperately need tenderness while you are busy proving your point.
And if you are the wounded one reading this, hear something equally important:
Biblical mutuality does not require you to call evil good.
Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened.
Reconciliation is not identical to ignoring danger.
And repentance worthy of trust produces fruit.
Jesus Christ does not heal marriages by teaching people better ways to hide darkness.
He brings darkness into the light.
Perhaps this article exposed something.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is not showing you this so you can send it angrily to your spouse.
Maybe He is showing it to you first.
Ask the terrifying question:
“Lord, what in me needs to change?”
Not:
“Lord, show my spouse how wrong they are.”
Start here.
With me.
Search me.
Correct me.
Break whatever selfishness I have baptized as biblical.
Heal whatever wound I have allowed to become bitterness.
Teach me to love like Christ.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to write your entire story publicly. But don't disappear into silence either.

Or, if God has already restored something you once believed was beyond repair, tell your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that broken chapters do not have to become final chapters.
Not because every sentence will be easy to hear tomorrow.
Because some truths need to be read again after the emotions settle.
That simple share also helps this ministry carry Scripture-centered content beyond the people we could reach alone.
It doesn't.
It cannot.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior is a requirement for glorifying God.
Scripture does not give us the authority to make that claim.
The New Testament teaches voluntary generosity rather than giving “under compulsion.”
Give Jesus more than your money.
Give Him the locked room.
The resentment.
The secret browser history.
The wounded sexuality.
The pride.
The coldness.
The shame.
The marriage everybody thinks is perfect.
The marriage you fear is dying.
The memory you cannot erase.
The apology you have refused to make.
The forgiveness you are struggling to understand.
Bring Him the scandal.
Because Jesus has never been frightened by the chapters we are ashamed to let anybody read.
He walked toward sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He confronted hypocrites.
He restored failures.
He carried shame to a Roman cross.
And He walked out of a tomb.
That means your worst chapter does not have to possess the pen forever.
There is grace for the spouse who was selfish.
Grace for the spouse who is wounded.
Grace for the marriage that needs rebuilding.
Grace for the person who must finally tell the truth.
Grace for repentance.
Grace for forgiveness.
Grace for transformation.
Not cheap grace that excuses darkness.
Cross-shaped grace that drags darkness into the light and teaches broken people how to become new.
So tonight, before you ask whether your spouse is giving you everything marriage says you deserve...
stand beneath the cross and ask whether you are becoming the kind of person who gives love the way Christ has loved you.
Because perhaps the question was never merely:
“What does my spouse owe me?”
Perhaps the deeper question has always been:
“Now that I belong to Jesus... what would it look like for Christ to teach me how to love?”
The Gospel does not give selfishness a Bible verse to hide behind; it brings selfishness to the cross so Jesus can teach two wounded people how to love again.
